description: Patterns for detecting and interpreting correlations, including business impact and leakage risks

correlation_patterns.name: Near-Perfect Positive Correlation
correlation_patterns.interpretation: These features are essentially duplicates — one can be predicted almost perfectly from the other.
possible_causes: One is derived from the other (total = quantity × price)
Same metric in different units (kg vs lbs)
Data entry artifact (same source column copied)
correlation_patterns.action: Drop one. If one might be target leakage, investigate immediately. Keep the more interpretable feature.
correlation_patterns.business_impact: Redundant features inflate model complexity and can cause unstable coefficients in linear models.
correlation_patterns.example: Correlation between 'total_amount' and 'subtotal_after_tax' is 0.98 — 'total_amount' appears to be derived from 'subtotal'. Keeping 'subtotal_after_tax' as the primary feature.

correlation_patterns.name: Strong Positive Correlation
correlation_patterns.interpretation: Strong linear relationship but not perfectly redundant. May share underlying cause.
correlation_patterns.action: Keep both but flag as correlated pair. Consider PCA or feature selection if model is linear.
correlation_patterns.example: Age and years_at_company have correlation 0.72 — naturally correlated (older employees tend to have longer tenure). Both provide value but should be monitored for multicollinearity.

correlation_patterns.name: Moderate Correlation
correlation_patterns.interpretation: Meaningful relationship exists but features capture different aspects. Usually safe to keep both.
correlation_patterns.action: No action needed. Note the relationship for business insights.
correlation_patterns.example: Income and education_level have correlation 0.55 — expected relationship that provides useful context for segment analysis.

correlation_patterns.name: Unexpected Zero Correlation
correlation_patterns.interpretation: Features that SHOULD be correlated but aren't — this may indicate data quality issues or non-linear relationships.
correlation_patterns.detection: Domain knowledge suggests correlation should exist (e.g., sales vs marketing spend)
correlation_patterns.action: Investigate: check for data errors, non-linear relationships, confounding variables, or segmented effects.
correlation_patterns.example: ⚠️ Marketing_spend and revenue show near-zero correlation (0.03) — this is suspicious. Investigation reveals: marketing data is lagged by 2 months, masking the true relationship.

correlation_patterns.name: Suspicious Correlation with Target (Leakage Risk)
correlation_patterns.interpretation: Feature correlates too strongly with the target variable — almost certainly leakage or derivation.
correlation_patterns.action: IMMEDIATELY investigate. Check if this feature is available at prediction time. If not → remove immediately.
correlation_patterns.example: ⚠️ CRITICAL LEAKAGE RISK: Feature 'account_status' has 0.94 correlation with target 'churn'. Investigation: 'account_status' is set to 'cancelled' AFTER churn happens — this IS the target, not a predictor.

correlation_patterns.name: Strong Negative Correlation
correlation_patterns.interpretation: Inverse relationship — as one increases, the other decreases. May indicate complementary features.
correlation_patterns.action: Verify the relationship makes domain sense. If one is the inverse of the other (satisfaction vs complaints), consider dropping one.
correlation_patterns.example: Customer_satisfaction and complaint_count have correlation -0.78 — logically consistent inverse relationship. Keep both; they provide different operational perspectives.

heatmap_interpretation_guide.how_to_read: The correlation heatmap shows pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between all numeric features. Values range from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive). 0 means no linear relationship.
what_to_look_for: Bright red blocks off-diagonal → redundant feature pairs to investigate
Bright red in the target column → strong predictors (or leakage risks)
Bright blue in the target column → inverse predictors
White rows/columns → features with no linear relationships (may still have non-linear ones)
